This is an upright piano with its front panels and lid off: 88 keys, three pedals, 229 strings (as modelled here), and the action, the levers that link each key to its hammer and damper. It follows a Yamaha U1, 152 × 122 × 61 cm [[1](#ref-1)], with standard key widths [[14](#ref-14), [15](#ref-15)]. Strike a key and the graphs show its string moving and each mode's strength; the sound is computed live from a stiff-string model. Made in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.

To play, hold a key in the 3D view or on the strip below and let go to damp it; on a computer, A to ' play an octave, Z and X shift it, and Space holds the sustain pedal.

## What you are seeing

**The hammer starts the modes.** A string fixed at both ends moves as a sum of modes, shapes sin(nπx/L) each swinging at its own frequency. The jack, a lever in each key's action, throws the hammer and slips out from under it, so the hammer hits the string in free flight and falls back at once [[19](#ref-19)]. That push sets how strongly each mode rings; once the hammer has left the string, it cannot add a frequency the string does not already have (in this linear model). Books commonly give 1/7 to 1/9 of the way along, though on modern pianos many notes are struck nearer the end, at 1/12 to 1/17 [[11](#ref-11)]; the model uses 1/8, a node (a point that does not move) of modes 8 and 16, which stay silent.

**The damper.** Releasing a key returns a felt damper to its strings, just below the hammer [[7](#ref-7)]. To a good approximation, each mode then dies at a rate set by how much it moves under the felt (the orange ticks); the felt covers about 5 cm of string (less on short strings), so every mode is caught. Pianos leave about the top octave and a half undamped, as those short strings die quickly [[12](#ref-12), [13](#ref-13)]; this model leaves the top 20 keys, F6 to C8.

**The three pedals.** On an upright the left (soft) pedal moves the hammer rail toward the strings, so the hammers swing a shorter way and land more gently. The middle (practice mute) pedal drops a felt strip between hammers and strings. The right (sustain) pedal lifts every damper [[1](#ref-1), [8](#ref-8), [9](#ref-9), [10](#ref-10)]. None changes a string's tension or stiffness, so none changes its frequencies.

**The strings.** On a typical piano, and in this model, the lowest 10 notes have one string, the next 15 two, the rest three [[3](#ref-3)]; the bass strings are copper-wound [[2](#ref-2)] and overstrung, crossing the tenor strings on a bridge of their own [[6](#ref-6), [8](#ref-8), [10](#ref-10)].

**A stiff string.** Thick steel wire also resists bending, which puts each partial (each frequency in the note) slightly sharp of a whole-number multiple, $f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + B n^2}$ [[5](#ref-5)], where f₀ is the frequency the string would have without stiffness. B is least mid-keyboard and grows toward both ends [[16](#ref-16), [17](#ref-17)]. Tuners therefore stretch octaves slightly wider than 2 : 1 [[18](#ref-18)], which reduces the beating (a slow wobble in loudness) between the lower note's sharp partials and the note above [[17](#ref-17), [20](#ref-20)].

Left out: each note is one ideal stiff string with pinned ends, with no coupling between strings and no soundboard resonances. The hammer is a brief push at one point (its felt's nonlinearity is ignored); the damper felt is a uniform strip. B and the decay times are chosen by hand, not measured, and B here only rises toward the treble. String lengths other than the longest (119 cm) and a parlour grand's shortest string (5.2 cm) [[1](#ref-1), [4](#ref-4)] are illustrative.

**Read more:** [The Shape of a Sound, post 3: the piano, and why tuners stretch octaves](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#piano).
